proposal: The Mandate recommends resizing humanitarian assistance by working with Congress on deep cuts to the International Disaster Assistance account, setting country exit strategies that limit how long responses run, and shifting awards from UN agencies, large international NGOs and contractors to local and faith-based organizations using fixed-amount awards, stricter diversion vetting and more burden-sharing by other donors. It also recommends extending the PEPFAR localization model across USAID and giving each mission a minimum share of its portfolio for local and new partners.
remaining: A mission-level minimum share for local and new partners and fixed-amount awards (pp. 263-264, 268-269): not found; the August 2026 awards went to US-based faith-based organizations and, in the health award, a coalition of local partners.
Country exit strategies that term-limit humanitarian responses (p. 268): not found; the OCHA arrangement's exit clauses are between the parties, not response limits.

Moving awards away from UN agencies (p. 268): the December 2025 arrangement routes about $2 billion through OCHA-managed pooled funds, and the US reportedly plans to route all humanitarian funding that way.
Conditioning US contributions on commitments from other donors (p. 269): referenced only as a factor in country-level agreements.

status_summary: The record shows resizing of humanitarian funding and a partial shift toward faith-based partners, along with one step that differs from the Mandate's recommendation to move awards away from UN agencies. USAID's remaining operations were merged into the State Department on 2025-07-01, by which time NPR reported more than 80 percent of its programs terminated, and the Rescissions Act (Public Law 119-28, 2025-07-24) rescinded $496 million of International Disaster Assistance and $800 million of Migration and Refugee Assistance. The FY2026 National Security, Department of State appropriations act, Division F of Public Law 119-75 (enacted 2026-02-03 per the govinfo.gov bill status and the Congressional Research Service), provides 5.50 billion dollars for two global humanitarian accounts: 5.40 billion for a new International Humanitarian Assistance account that carries the authorities of the former International Disaster Assistance and Migration and Refugee Assistance accounts, and 100 million for the Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance account. CRS states this is 25.8 percent below FY2025 enacted humanitarian assistance and above the Administration's request of 2.5 billion plus 1.5 billion dollars (37.5 percent higher than the request total). The U.S. Global Leadership Coalition, an advocacy group, reports roughly 37 percent below FY2025 using a broader set of accounts; its figure and CRS's were not reconciled. A supplemental request of 2026-06-24 sought a further 800 million dollars for the International Humanitarian Assistance account for Ebola response (CRS). On 2025-12-29 the United Nations and the US government signed a memorandum of understanding in Geneva under which the US commits $2 billion to UN-managed humanitarian funds covering 17 countries and the Central Emergency Response Fund (UN News); Capital FM reports the money moves through country-level pooled funds in place of project-based grants and stays open to UN and non-UN partners, and The New Humanitarian reports the US plans eventually to route all of its humanitarian funding through OCHA. On 2026-08-06 State announced nearly $2 billion for faith-based and community organizations, including $538 million for humanitarian response to Samaritan's Purse and a consortium led by World Vision and Compassion International, which are large US-based faith-based organizations rather than local entities, and a health award to World Vision with a consortium of local faith-based implementers (State's release was not reachable; DevelopmentAid reported it). Inference: the largest documented humanitarian channel, the $2 billion UN-managed arrangement, runs opposite to the Mandate's shift away from UN agencies, while the funding cuts align with it. On 2026-05-14 the UN Secretary-General's spokesperson welcomed an additional 1.8 billion dollars in U.S. humanitarian funding announced that day; the statement does not say how the money is routed or to whom it is awarded. No mission minimum for local partners, fixed-amount award policy, country exit strategies or explicit other-donor funding condition was found.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14169 paused foreign development assistance and required each program to be reviewed for consistency with US foreign policy (published 2025-01-30 at 90 FR 8619).
USAID's remaining operations are merged into the State Department as the agency closes; NPR reported that more than 80 percent of its programs had been terminated by then.

The Rescissions Act of 2025 rescinded $496 million of International Disaster Assistance, $800 million of Migration and Refugee Assistance, $57 million of Transition Initiatives and $43 million of the Complex Crises Fund.

The United Nations and the US government sign a memorandum of understanding in Geneva committing $2 billion to UN-managed humanitarian funds for 17 named countries (Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Ukraine, Haiti, Nigeria, Ethiopia, South Sudan, Mozambique, Myanmar, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Sudan, Bangladesh, Syria, Uganda, Kenya and Chad) and the Central Emergency Response Fund, per UN News; the Emergency Relief Coordinator says the deal does not mean agreement on every issue. Capital FM (via AllAfrica) reports the funds are country- and crisis-level pooled funds replacing earmarked project grants and stay open to UN and non-UN partners; The New Humanitarian reports the memorandum runs to 2027-12-31 with mutual exit clauses and that the US plans eventually to route all of its humanitarian funding through OCHA.

The FY2026 National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs appropriations act becomes law as Division F of Public Law 119-75 (H.R. 7148) after Senate passage 71 to 29 on 2026-01-30 and House agreement 217 to 214 on 2026-02-03 (govinfo.gov bill status). Per CRS it provides 5.50 billion dollars for two global humanitarian accounts (5.40 billion for International Humanitarian Assistance, which carries the authorities of the former International Disaster Assistance and Migration and Refugee Assistance accounts, and 100 million for Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance), 25.8 percent below FY2025 enacted and above the request of 2.5 billion plus 1.5 billion dollars; USGLC reports different comparison figures.

The United States announces an additional 1.8 billion dollars for humanitarian work by the UN and its partners, as described in a statement that day by the Spokesperson for the UN Secretary-General; the statement gives no routing or recipient detail.
timeline.source: United Nations, Spokesperson for the Secretary-General

timeline.event: The Administration transmits a supplemental funding request that includes 800 million dollars for the International Humanitarian Assistance account for Ebola response (CRS).

State announces nearly $2 billion in partnerships with faith-based and community organizations: $538 million for humanitarian response to Samaritan's Purse and a consortium led by World Vision and Compassion International (reaching a stated 7 million people in 16 crises), and about $1.4 billion for health services, including up to $850 million over five years to World Vision and a consortium of local faith-based implementers. State says at least 80 percent of health resources will reach frontline services.
